titleText.es: Se podría afirmar que este mismo recurso al distanciamiento irónico, participando al mismo tiempo de la cosa en cuestión, es la definición misma de hipsterismo contemporáneo. Pero, por otro lado, un momento, estás en una habitación vacía. ¿A quién le hablas?
titleText.en: You may point out that this very retreat into ironic detachment while still clearly participating in the thing in question is the very definition of contemporary hipsterdom. But on the other hand, wait, you're in an empty room. Who are you talking to?

applications.explanationEn: Petardo follows ombliguismo and describes the navel-gazing as tiresome.
Petardo takes masculine singular form to match ombliguismo.
Por parte de introduces gente as the source responsible for the attitude.
Insegura follows gente and describes those people.
Insegura is feminine singular because the collective noun gente is feminine singular.
Que refers back to gráficas, and empeoran states what those graphs do; lo supplies the affected situation between them.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Hipster is a loanword used in Spanish for someone associated with deliberately alternative, fashionable, or non-mainstream tastes. The plural keeps the English-looking spelling hipsters.

example.es: Ese barrio atrae a muchos hipsters.
example.en: That neighborhood attracts many hipsters.

cards.questionEn: What progression do the rising curves satirize?
cards.answerEn: Each later curve represents a more self-aware complaint about hipsters, ending with a graph that complains about the whole chain and thereby adds yet another level.
cards.noteEn: The chart moves from seeing hipsters, to complaints about them, to complaints about the repeated word, and then to complaints that all such meta-commentary is the same insecure navel-gazing. The final curve says that graphs make everything worse, but that graph is itself another example. The similarly rising curves visualize an escalating loop of ironic detachment.
Continuo describes something that keeps recurring or carries on. This adjective is written without an accent; continuó with an accent would be a past verb form.

example.es: El continuo ruido resulta molesto.
example.en: The continual noise is annoying.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Here uso names the act or amount of using something. The same spelling can also be a verb meaning “I use,” so the surrounding words determine which meaning applies.

example.es: El uso del teléfono está prohibido.
example.en: Phone use is prohibited.

cards.questionEn: How do you criticize both the use and excessive use of something?
cards.answerEn: Use uso y abuso de followed by the thing being used.
cards.noteEn: Uso is ordinary use, while abuso intensifies the idea to overuse or misuse. The two nouns form a conventional pairing, and de introduces their object.

example.es: El artículo analiza el uso y abuso de las estadísticas.
example.en: The article analyzes the use and abuse of statistics.

cards.noteEn: With a word or expression, abuso can mean using it excessively until it becomes tiresome.

example.es: Criticaron el abuso de esa expresión.
example.en: They criticized the overuse of that expression.

cards.noteEn: Hipster is an English loanword used in Spanish for a person linked to deliberately alternative tastes or style.

example.es: La revista describe un estilo hipster.
example.en: The magazine describes a hipster style.

cards.answerEn: that; about the fact that (after queja)
cards.noteEn: After queja, de can introduce the content of the complaint. English often uses ‘that’ rather than translating de separately.

example.es: Hubo quejas de que faltaba información.
example.en: There were complaints that information was missing.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.es: Creo que Ana viene.
example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Before a singular noun without an article, todo can cover every instance of that kind. This differs from standalone todo, ‘everything.’

example.es: Todo nivel requiere práctica.
example.en: Every level requires practice.

cards.answerEn: meta-; about itself or a higher level of the same subject
cards.noteEn: The prefix meta- forms words for something that comments on, describes, or operates at a level above the original thing. It may be shown separately before a hyphen when its parts are being emphasized.

example.es: La novela incluye un metacomentario sobre su propia historia.
example.en: The novel includes meta-commentary about its own story.

cards.noteEn: Una opinión is a belief or judgment rather than an established fact.

example.es: Ana explicó su opinión sobre el proyecto.
example.en: Ana explained her opinion about the project.

cards.noteEn: Suponer can mean “to suppose,” but it also describes the result, amount, or consequence that something represents.

example.es: El cambio supone una hora más.
example.en: The change means one extra hour.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.es: Necesito una taza de café.
example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.noteEn: Ombligo means ‘navel.’ Ombliguismo figuratively criticizes excessive attention to oneself or one's own small circle.

example.es: El ensayo critica el ombliguismo del sector.
example.en: The essay criticizes the sector's navel-gazing.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.es: Necesito una mochila nueva.
example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.noteEn: In informal Spanish, petardo can describe a person or thing that is a bore or a pain. As an adjective, its ending follows the noun it describes.

example.es: Fue un discurso bastante petardo.
example.en: It was a pretty tiresome speech.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por parte de

cards.promptEs: por parte de + persona o grupo
cards.questionEn: How do you formally identify the person or group responsible for an action, judgment, or reaction?
cards.answerEn: Use por parte de followed by the person or group.
cards.noteEn: The expression often corresponds to English “on the part of” or, in some sentences, simply “by.” It highlights the source or responsible side rather than a physical part.

example.es: Hubo un error por parte del banco.
example.en: There was an error on the bank's part.

cards.noteEn: In the formal expression por parte de, parte helps identify the person or group responsible for an action, judgment, or reaction.

example.es: Fue un error por parte del equipo.
example.en: It was a mistake on the team's part.

cards.noteEn: Insegura is feminine singular. Spanish describing words agree with the grammatical gender and number of what they describe.

example.es: La gente insegura busca aprobación.
example.en: Insecure people seek approval.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.es: La película, la vimos ayer.
example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.answerEn: they make it worse; they worsen
cards.noteEn: Empeoran is a plural present form of empeorar. With lo before it, lo stands for the situation being made worse.

example.es: Esos cambios lo empeoran.
example.en: Those changes make it worse.

cards.noteEn: Actualidad refers to what is current now. It does not mean the English word ‘actuality.’

example.es: El gráfico llega hasta la actualidad.
example.en: The graph reaches the present day.
